title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Richmond, VA | Genstone
metaDescription: Richmond investor rehabs for Fan rowhouses, Church Hill brick, Northside frame and Southside ranches: scopes, draws, permits and local crews.
intro:
Richmond rewards investors who understand old brick. Much of the city's buyable inventory was built before the Second World War, in attached and semi-attached rows that share walls, roof drainage and sometimes a sewer lateral with the house next door. A rehab here is rarely a simple paint-and-flooring job, and the estimate has to see through plaster to the wiring, the box gutters and the crawlspace before you commit to a number.

Genstone Construction works for investors, lenders and servicers who buy in Richmond and need a contractor that prices the hidden work up front. We start with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, write a line-item scope with a draw schedule tied to completed work, and assign one field manager who coordinates vetted, licensed local trades through permits, historic review where it applies, and final inspection. You see progress and documentation without driving to the job, and you pay nothing up front.
housingStock:
Richmond's housing reads like a timeline laid out on a map. The oldest stock sits east of downtown in Church Hill and Union Hill, where Greek Revival and Italianate brick rowhouses from the nineteenth century line streets that climb above Shockoe Bottom. Jackson Ward, just north of downtown, holds a dense run of ornamented brick and frame townhouses with cast-iron porches. West of Belvidere, the Fan District and the Museum District filled in during the late 1800s and early 1900s with two- and three-story attached brick homes, many with low-slope rear roofs, front parapets, box gutters hidden behind cornices and narrow rear yards reached by alleys.

North of the James, the streetcar suburbs of Barton Heights, Highland Park, Bellevue and Ginter Park are mostly detached frame and brick houses from roughly the 1900s through the 1930s: foursquares, bungalows and Colonial Revival homes on brick piers or continuous brick foundations with crawlspaces. Across the river, Woodland Heights, Forest Hill and Manchester carry a similar early-twentieth-century mix, while much of Southside beyond Forest Hill Avenue is postwar brick ranches and Cape Cods on crawlspaces.

For a rehab budget, that history means a few predictable things. Plaster on wood lath is the default wall finish in anything prewar, and opening it to rewire turns into a patching or drywall decision. Knob-and-tube wiring still turns up in Fan and Northside houses, as do galvanized supply lines and cast-iron drains. Brick party walls need repointing with a lime-compatible mortar rather than hard modern mix, or the brick spalls. Slate and standing-seam metal roofs survive on some older homes and are worth repairing rather than tearing off when the visible front matters to buyers. And because most houses sit over crawlspaces rather than full basements, moisture, sagging joists and termite damage are inspection items on nearly every property.

commonIssues.title: Box gutters and low-slope rear roofs
commonIssues.body: Many Fan and Museum District rowhouses drain through built-in box gutters behind the cornice and a flat or low-slope roof at the back. When the liner fails, water runs into the cornice, the top of the brick wall and the ceiling below. We scope box gutter relining and rear-roof membrane replacement as a distinct line item, because a fresh ceiling under a failed gutter will stain again before the house sells or appraises.

commonIssues.title: Crawlspace moisture and termite damage
commonIssues.body: Richmond's humid summers and clay soils keep crawlspaces damp, and subterranean termites are a routine finding in older frame and brick homes alike. Expect sill plate and joist repairs, sistering, new vapor barrier, and sometimes drainage or a dehumidifier. Getting under the house during the pre-offer review is the only way to know whether a level floor upstairs is real or hiding rot on the sills.

commonIssues.title: Knob-and-tube and undersized service
commonIssues.body: Prewar houses in Northside, Church Hill and the Fan still surface knob-and-tube circuits, ungrounded outlets and older panels too small for a modern kitchen and central air. Insurers and lenders frequently balk at live knob-and-tube. A full rewire through plaster walls is labor-heavy, so we price access, fishing routes and plaster repair together instead of treating the electrical bid as a standalone number.

commonIssues.title: Soft brick and failing mortar
commonIssues.body: Nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century Richmond brick is softer than modern brick, and repointing it with hard Portland-heavy mortar traps moisture and breaks the faces off. Party walls, chimneys and parapets need lime-compatible mortar and patience. In a historic district, the masonry approach also has to satisfy design review, so we write mortar type and joint profile into the scope rather than leaving it to a crew's habit.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint on porches and trim
commonIssues.body: Almost every house built before 1978 in the city carries lead-based paint somewhere, usually on porch columns, window sashes, door casings and exterior trim. Any work that disturbs it in a rental or a home with children falls under EPA renovation rules, which means certified renovators, containment and cleaning verification. That affects both schedule and cost on porch restorations, window work and exterior paint, so it belongs in the estimate from day one.

investorMarket:
Investor activity in Richmond splits roughly along the river and the old streetcar lines. The Fan, Museum District and Church Hill are retail flip territory: buyers there pay for restored original detail, and a house with intact heart pine floors, working fireplaces and a modern kitchen in a sympathetic style competes well. Margins come from buying the tired house on a good block, not from cutting finish quality, because comparable sales in those neighborhoods are restored homes.

Northside neighborhoods like Highland Park, Barton Heights and Bellevue offer a wider spread. Some blocks support resale to first-time buyers, and others work better as rentals held through a BRRRR cycle, with durable finishes chosen to appraise well without overbuilding. Southside, including Woodland Heights, Swansboro and the postwar ranch areas south of Forest Hill Avenue, tends to suit single-family rental portfolios, since brick ranches on crawlspaces are simple to standardize.

Student demand from Virginia Commonwealth University keeps Oregon Hill, Randolph and the eastern Fan interesting for small multifamily and converted-rowhouse rentals, where durability and fire separation matter more than designer finishes. Across the city line, Henrico and Chesterfield add newer suburban inventory that is easier to renovate but competes with new construction, so the scope there leans toward kitchens, baths and systems rather than structure.
permits:
Building permits in the city are issued through the City of Richmond Department of Planning and Development Review, which handles plan review and inspections under the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code. Structural repairs, additions, new or relocated walls, electrical rewiring, plumbing replacement, HVAC changeouts, and roof work beyond simple repair generally require permits, with rough-in and final inspections for each trade.

The bigger local variable is historic review. Church Hill, Union Hill, Jackson Ward, the St. John's Church area, Monument Avenue and several other areas are City Old and Historic Districts, where exterior changes visible from the street need a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Commission of Architecture and Historic Review. That covers windows, doors, porches, roofing materials, siding and masonry, and it adds time before work can start. The commission does not review interior work.

In Virginia, contractors must hold a license from the Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation's Board for Contractors at the class matching the job size. Genstone coordinates licensed local contractors and handles permit applications, inspection scheduling and lien waivers as part of every project.
climate:
Richmond sits in a humid subtropical zone with long, sticky summers and short winters that still bring hard freezes, occasional ice storms and the odd heavy snow. Summer is the hardest season on crawlspaces and attics, and it is when you discover undersized or tired air conditioning, so we schedule HVAC replacement and duct sealing early in a summer rehab rather than at the end.

Afternoon thunderstorms in summer and remnants of tropical systems in late summer and fall test roofs, box gutters and grading. A roof or gutter leak that seems minor at the walkthrough can become a ceiling repair after one storm, which is why we dry in the house before interior finishes. Low areas such as Shockoe Bottom have a long flood history from the James River and local drainage. Exterior paint and masonry work is easiest in spring and fall, when temperatures and humidity let mortar and coatings cure properly.

faqs.q: Do you handle Certificate of Appropriateness applications in Richmond's historic districts?
faqs.a: Yes. When a property sits in a City Old and Historic District such as Church Hill or Jackson Ward, the scope identifies exterior items that need review, like windows, porch rebuilds, roofing or masonry, and we prepare the application with the photos and specifications the Commission of Architecture and Historic Review expects. Planning for review up front keeps your interior trades moving while the exterior approval is pending, instead of stopping the whole job.

faqs.q: Is a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review useful on a Fan rowhouse I have not bought yet?
faqs.a: That is exactly when it helps most. A Fan rowhouse can look cosmetic and still need a box gutter relining, a rear roof, rewiring and joist repairs in the crawlspace. The review estimates those costs, checks your after-repair value against restored comparables, and tells you whether the numbers support your offer before you commit capital. You walk into negotiation knowing which problems are priced into the asking price and which are not.

faqs.q: How do draws work on a Richmond renovation?
faqs.a: There is no upfront payment. The estimate includes a draw schedule broken into milestones such as demolition and dry-in, rough-ins and inspections, and finishes. When a milestone is complete and documented, that draw is billed. The last payment waits until the house is finished and you have signed off. Lenders and servicers who fund draws themselves receive the same documentation, so inspections and draw releases line up without extra back-and-forth.

faqs.q: Do you work in Henrico and Chesterfield as well as the city?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone coordinates vetted, licensed contractors across the Richmond region, including Henrico County and Chesterfield County, plus nearby towns like Mechanicsville and Glen Allen. The counties run their own permit offices with their own review timing, and their housing is generally newer, so the scope tends to shift from structural and masonry work toward kitchens, baths, flooring and mechanical updates. The same field manager model and draw structure apply.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Richmond, VA | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Flip renovations in Richmond priced for restored-home comps in the Fan, Church Hill and Northside, with draws tied to finished work and one field manager.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Richmond
fix-flip.intro:
Selling a renovated house in Richmond means competing with neighbors who restored theirs carefully. In the Fan, the Museum District and Church Hill, buyers walk in comparing your heart pine floors, mantels and plaster crown against the house down the block that kept every original detail. On Northside and in Woodland Heights the comparison is gentler, but buyers still notice when a flipper covered old character with builder-grade shortcuts.

Genstone Construction builds flip scopes around the comparable sales that will set your price. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the work you can see and the work behind the plaster, so the after-repair value you underwrite is grounded in what restored homes nearby actually sold for. One field manager runs the job, licensed local trades do the work, and draws follow completed milestones.

sections.body:
On a Fan or Museum District flip, the money that moves price is in the front rooms, the kitchen and the primary bath. Refinishing original heart pine instead of covering it, restoring mantels, and keeping or reproducing plaster crown signal quality to buyers who know these houses. Kitchens that open to the rear room without erasing the original floor plan tend to show better than gutted open layouts that feel out of place behind a nineteenth-century facade.

Northside buyers in Highland Park, Bellevue and Ginter Park often want a little more square footage and modern flow, so a finished attic, a second bath or a reworked rear addition can matter more than restored trim. In Southside ranch neighborhoods, clean, durable mid-range finishes and a strong exterior first impression are usually enough.

We write the scope in two or three finish levels where the comps support it, so you can see what moving from a standard to a restored-detail package costs against the price difference in recent sales on your block.

sections.h2: The hidden items that sink Richmond flip budgets
sections.body:
Richmond flips rarely go over budget on cabinets. They go over on box gutters, rear roofs, crawlspace framing and wiring discovered after demolition. A rowhouse that looked dry in March can show a leaking box gutter in the first July storm, staining fresh plaster upstairs. Knob-and-tube found during the kitchen demo can turn a partial electrical upgrade into a whole-house rewire through plaster walls.

We price those risks before you buy. The pre-offer review includes a look at the roof drainage, the crawlspace, the panel and visible wiring, and the supply and drain lines. Where something cannot be confirmed without opening a wall, we carry an allowance and say so plainly, rather than burying it.

Buyer inspections in these neighborhoods are thorough, and inspectors who work the Fan and Church Hill know where to look. Fixing the roof drainage, sills and wiring during the rehab costs less than a renegotiation after an inspection report lands in the middle of your closing timeline.

sections.h2: Keeping carry costs down through permits and review
sections.body:
Carrying costs on a Richmond flip are driven by two clocks: permit review at the Department of Planning and Development Review, and historic review if the house sits in an Old and Historic District. A Church Hill flip that needs new windows or a rebuilt porch cannot start that exterior work until the Commission of Architecture and Historic Review approves it.

We sequence around those clocks. Interior demolition, framing repairs, rough-ins and inspections proceed while exterior applications are in review, so the house is not sitting idle. Porch and window specifications are written to match what the commission typically approves, which reduces back-and-forth.

Draws are tied to milestones like dry-in, passed rough-in inspections and finished kitchen, and your field manager posts photos and inspection results so you can track the job without visiting. When the work is done and you have approved it, we bill the final payment, and the house goes to market with permits closed and documentation ready for the buyer's agent.

faqs.q: Can you restore original details on a Fan District flip instead of replacing them?
faqs.a: Yes, and in the Fan it often pays. Refinishing heart pine floors, repairing plaster crown, restoring mantels and keeping original doors usually cost less than buyers assume they add in value. Our scope separates restoration items from replacement items so you can choose. Where an original element is too far gone, we specify a replacement that matches the profile and scale of the house rather than a generic big-box product.

faqs.q: What does a typical Richmond flip scope include that a suburban flip might not?
faqs.a: Expect line items for box gutter relining, rear low-slope roof replacement, repointing with lime-compatible mortar, crawlspace framing and vapor barrier, plaster repair after rewiring, and lead-safe work practices on porches and trim. Suburban flips in Henrico or Chesterfield usually skip most of those and focus on kitchens, baths and flooring. Knowing which list applies is what keeps a Richmond rowhouse budget honest.

faqs.q: How do you handle a Church Hill flip that needs historic approval?
faqs.a: We identify exterior work that needs a Certificate of Appropriateness during the pre-offer review, then prepare the application with photos and specifications. Interior work, which is not reviewed, starts while the application is pending. That keeps your timeline moving and avoids the common mistake of installing windows or siding before approval and then being told to remove them. Window repair instead of replacement is often the faster path.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Richmond, VA | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR rehabs in Richmond built for the refinance appraisal and long tenancy, from Northside foursquares to Southside brick ranches on crawlspaces.
brrrr.intro:
A BRRRR deal in Richmond lives or dies on two numbers: what the appraiser says the house is worth after the rehab, and what it costs to keep the place rented for years. Northside foursquares, Southside brick ranches and Manchester frame houses can all work, but each asks a different scope to get to a refinance appraisal without spending money a tenant will wear out.

Genstone Construction writes BRRRR scopes for both goals. The free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs and tests the after-repair value against recent sales the appraiser is likely to pull. The scope then puts money into systems, roof, structure and finishes that hold up to tenants. Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans, so when it suits your plan the refinance side can be discussed alongside the rehab.

sections.h2: Renovating to the Richmond refinance appraisal
sections.body:
Appraisers in Richmond lean on recent renovated sales within the same neighborhood, and the gap between blocks can be wide. A house in Highland Park or Barton Heights may sit next to a fully restored comparable on one street and a tired rental on the next. Before scoping finishes, we look at which sales are likely to be used and what condition they were in.

The items that move an appraisal here are usually bedroom and bathroom count, a functional kitchen, central air, and a sound roof and foundation. Adding a second full bath in a Northside foursquare, or finishing an attic room with legal egress, can change the comparable set entirely. Designer tile and premium fixtures rarely do.

We document the work with photos, permits and final inspection sign-offs so the appraiser and your lender have a clear record of what was replaced. A permitted rewire, new HVAC and new roof carry more weight when the paperwork is in hand than when an appraiser has to take a seller's word.

sections.h2: Rental-grade materials for Richmond's older houses
sections.body:
Durability matters more than polish in a hold, and older Richmond houses have their own wear points. Original heart pine floors are worth refinishing where they are sound, because they outlast most replacement flooring. Where floors are patched or uneven, luxury vinyl plank over a leveled subfloor is easier to maintain between tenants.

Plaster walls can stay in rooms that do not need rewiring; drywall goes where walls are opened. Kitchens get solid-surface or quartz counters and cabinets that survive turnovers. Bathrooms get tile surrounds or one-piece shower units rather than painted drywall that blisters in humid summers.

Crawlspaces get a proper vapor barrier and, where moisture is chronic, drainage or dehumidification, since a damp crawl in Richmond means mold complaints, pest calls and soft floors within a few years. Exterior wood on porches is repaired and painted with lead-safe practices, and gutters and downspouts are routed away from the foundation to keep the clay soil around the house from staying saturated.

sections.h2: Choosing BRRRR houses by Richmond neighborhood
sections.body:
Not every part of the city behaves the same in a BRRRR cycle. Southside brick ranches built after the war are among the easiest to standardize: one level, crawlspace access, simple roofs and predictable mechanical layouts. They appraise from a steady set of comparables and rent to long-term tenants.

Northside frame houses offer more square footage and more appreciation potential but carry more structural and electrical risk. Manchester and Swansboro bring a mix of older frame homes where renovation can add meaningful value, but the appraisal case depends on finding renovated comparables nearby.

Near VCU, Oregon Hill and Randolph homes rent well to students but turn over more often, which shifts the scope toward hard-wearing finishes and away from details. We help you match the house to the strategy during the pre-offer review, and if the numbers do not support a refinance at the price you are being asked, we tell you before you buy rather than after the appraisal comes back short.

faqs.q: What Richmond upgrades tend to help a BRRRR refinance appraisal?
faqs.a: Adding a bathroom or a legal bedroom, replacing old HVAC with central air, and fixing the roof and structure usually carry the most weight with Richmond appraisers, because they change which comparables apply and how the house is rated. Cosmetic upgrades beyond clean, durable mid-range finishes seldom move the number much. We weigh each item against the comparable sales most likely to be pulled for your block.

faqs.q: Should I keep original plaster in a Richmond rental?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Sound plaster is durable, quiet between rooms and costs nothing to keep. Where rewiring or plumbing work opens walls, we replace those sections with drywall rather than patching large areas. The scope notes which walls stay and which get opened, so you are not surprised by a full drywall bill midway through the rehab. Cracked but attached plaster can usually be stabilized and skim-coated for less.

faqs.q: Can Genstone Financial help with the refinance on a Richmond BRRRR?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans, which are often used for the refinance step after a rehab. Whether a loan fits depends on the property, the rent and your situation, so the conversation happens directly with Genstone Financial. Our role is to deliver the renovation and the documentation an appraiser and lender will want to see, including permits, final inspections and a photo record of every replaced system.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Richmond, VA | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Single-family rental rehabs in Richmond with portfolio finish standards, crawlspace and HVAC fixes, lead-safe work and tenant-ready turnovers.
rental-renovation.intro:
Running single-family rentals in Richmond means owning houses that range from century-old frame on Northside to brick ranches south of Forest Hill Avenue. A standard that works for one rarely works for the other without adjustment, and the city's humid summers punish shortcuts in crawlspaces, bathrooms and HVAC.

Genstone Construction renovates rental homes for individual landlords, funds and portfolio operators who want consistent finish standards and fewer maintenance calls. We write scopes against your spec sheet, flag where an older Richmond house needs something your spec does not cover, and coordinate licensed local trades through permits and inspections. Genstone Field Services also handles turns and make-ready work, which helps when a property cycles back after a lease ends.

sections.h2: Applying a portfolio standard to Richmond's mixed housing
sections.body:
Portfolio specs are usually written with slab-on-grade suburban homes in mind. Richmond houses push back on that template. A Northside foursquare has plaster walls, a crawlspace, an older electrical service and sometimes radiators. A Southside ranch has a crawlspace, possibly aluminum branch wiring if built in the late 1960s or early 1970s, and original windows.

We adapt your standard rather than abandoning it. Flooring, paint colors, fixtures, hardware and appliance packages stay consistent across the portfolio so your maintenance team stocks one set of parts. The house-specific items, like crawlspace encapsulation, panel upgrades, window replacement or plaster repair, are listed separately so you can see what the building itself demands.

That separation also helps underwriting: you can compare one Richmond rental to another on the standard package, then look at the building-specific line items to understand why one address costs more than its neighbor. Over several acquisitions, that record also shows which Richmond neighborhoods and house types carry the heaviest building-specific costs, which is useful when deciding where to buy next.

sections.h2: Cutting maintenance calls in a humid city
sections.body:
The most common tenant calls in Richmond rentals trace back to moisture and heat. Bath fans that vent into the attic instead of outside, damp crawlspaces that breed musty smells and pests, and old heat pumps that cannot keep up in July all generate calls in the first year of a lease.

We address those at renovation, when walls and floors are open. Bath fans get ducted to the exterior. Crawlspaces get vapor barriers and, where needed, sealed vents and dehumidification. HVAC systems are sized for the house, and ductwork in crawlspaces and attics gets sealed and insulated so the system is not cooling the crawl.

Gutters, downspout extensions and grading that sheds water away from the foundation round out the moisture package. On older houses, this group of items often matters more to long-term operating cost than any finish choice, because it determines whether the house stays dry and comfortable or slowly deteriorates between turns.

sections.h2: Lead-safe work and Richmond rental compliance
sections.body:
Most Richmond rental stock was built before 1978, so lead-based paint is a working assumption rather than a surprise. Renovation, repair and painting work that disturbs painted surfaces in pre-1978 rentals falls under the EPA's Renovation, Repair and Painting rule, which requires certified firms and renovators, containment and cleaning verification.

We plan for that on every older property. Window replacement, porch repair, door and trim work and exterior painting are scoped with lead-safe practices and the related documentation, which is part of the file you keep for the property. Doing it right during a renovation also reduces the chance that deteriorating paint becomes a code or health complaint after a tenant moves in.

Permits for electrical, plumbing, mechanical and structural work go through the city's Department of Planning and Development Review, and we close them out before handing the house back so your property manager inherits a clean record. Open permits left behind on a rental tend to resurface at the worst time, usually during a sale or refinance.

faqs.q: Can you match our existing rental spec across several Richmond houses?
faqs.a: Yes. We build the scope from your finish and fixture standards so every Richmond home in your portfolio uses the same flooring, paint, fixtures and appliances. Building-specific repairs like crawlspace work, panel upgrades or plaster repair appear as separate line items. That way your maintenance team stocks one set of parts and your asset managers can compare properties on equal terms.

faqs.q: Do you handle turns between tenants as well as full renovations?
faqs.a: Genstone Field Services handles turn and make-ready work, occupied maintenance, inspections and code compliance, while Genstone Construction handles larger renovations. For Richmond landlords that means one family of companies can carry a property from initial rehab through later turnovers, with the original scope and photos on file to speed up future work. Knowing which flooring, paint and fixtures went into a house makes each later turn faster to price and order.

faqs.q: What HVAC approach works for older Richmond rentals?
faqs.a: It depends on the house. Some older homes have hydronic radiators and no ductwork, where ductless mini-splits avoid tearing into plaster. Others have existing ducts in a crawlspace that only need sealing and a properly sized heat pump. We specify the system that fits the building and keeps tenant comfort complaints low during Richmond's long humid summers. Dehumidification capacity matters as much as cooling here.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex and 2–4 Unit Renovation in Richmond, VA | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Renovating Richmond duplexes, converted rowhouses and small walk-ups in the Fan, Oregon Hill and Northside, with separation, utilities and occupied phasing.
multifamily-renovation.intro:
Small multifamily in Richmond rarely looks like a purpose-built fourplex. More often it is a Fan rowhouse split into an upstairs and downstairs flat, a Church Hill double sharing a center wall, a Northside foursquare carved into units decades ago, or a small brick walk-up near VCU. Each of those buildings carries old conversion decisions that may or may not meet current code.

Genstone Construction renovates two- to four-unit buildings for investors who want them to perform and pass inspection. Our scopes address fire separation between units, separate utilities where practical, egress, and shared systems like roofs, sewer laterals and gutters, along with finishes inside each unit. Where tenants are in place, we phase the work so the building keeps producing rent during the renovation.

sections.h2: Converted rowhouses and doubles in the Fan and Church Hill
sections.body:
Many two-unit buildings in the Fan, Museum District and Church Hill were single-family homes split into flats during the mid-twentieth century. The conversion quality varies widely. Some have proper separation between floors and a second exit; others share a single interior stair with no fire-rated assembly between units and a tangle of shared electrical and plumbing.

When we scope one of these buildings, the first questions are about legal use and life safety. Is the second unit recognized by the city, and what does separation between units need to look like after the renovation? Does each unit have compliant egress? Can electric and water be split, or will one meter remain?

Those answers shape everything else. Adding a fire-rated ceiling assembly, separate panels and a second exit costs more than refinishing floors, but it also makes the building insurable and financeable as a multi-unit property. Historic district rules still apply to visible exterior changes like added stairs or doors, so those go through review.

Oregon Hill, Randolph and the eastern edge of the Fan hold small multifamily buildings and converted houses that rent to Virginia Commonwealth University students and staff. Turnover is high and the academic calendar dictates when units are empty, so the renovation window is often the summer between leases.

Scopes for these buildings prioritize hard-wearing materials and simple maintenance. Luxury vinyl plank instead of carpet, solid-surface counters, durable doors and hardware, and bathrooms that can survive frequent cleaning by tenants who are not always careful. Smoke and carbon monoxide detection, egress windows in sleeping rooms and clear exit paths are non-negotiable, both for safety and because student housing draws attention from code enforcement.

We plan around the summer gap. Long-lead items like windows, cabinets and HVAC equipment are ordered before tenants move out, crews are booked in the spring, and inspections are scheduled so units are turned and ready before the fall move-in date. Missing that date can mean a unit sits empty for a full semester.

The expensive surprises in a Richmond small multifamily usually sit in shared systems. A single sewer lateral serving two units may be old clay or cast iron with root intrusion. A shared roof and box gutter may be leaking into the top unit. One aging boiler may heat several apartments.

We scope shared systems first, because they affect every unit. A camera inspection of the sewer lateral, a roof and gutter assessment and a look at the heating plant come before finish decisions. When the building is occupied, we sequence the work so shared-system replacement causes the shortest possible disruption, coordinating notices and access with your property manager.

Unit interiors are then renovated one at a time as vacancies allow, or all at once if the building is empty. Either way, each unit has its own draw milestones, and your field manager tracks permits and inspections so the building's rental income is not held up by an open permit on one apartment.

faqs.q: Can you split utilities in a converted Richmond rowhouse?
faqs.a: Often, but not always. Separating electric service is usually practical with a new meter base and panels, coordinated with the utility. Separating water and gas depends on the existing lines and the space available. We assess what is possible in the building during the pre-offer review and price each option, so you can weigh the cost against the benefit of tenants paying their own utilities.

faqs.q: Do you renovate occupied duplexes in Richmond?
faqs.a: Yes. We phase work so shared systems like the roof, sewer lateral or heating plant are handled with minimal disruption, and we renovate unit interiors as they become vacant. Your property manager receives schedules for any work affecting occupied units, and the field manager coordinates access so tenants are not surprised by trades at the door. Water or power shutoffs are scheduled in short, announced windows.

faqs.q: What fire separation work is common in Richmond multi-unit conversions?
faqs.a: Older conversions frequently lack a rated assembly between units and may rely on a single interior stair. Typical fixes include fire-rated ceilings or walls between units, rated doors at unit entries, interconnected smoke alarms and, where needed, a second means of egress. The exact requirement depends on the building and the code path the city applies to your project. We confirm it with plan review early.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Richmond, VA | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor for Richmond buyers, agents and lenders: Standard and Limited bids for prewar homes, consultant coordination and draws.
fha-203k.intro:
Richmond is full of houses that suit an FHA 203(k) loan: a Northside bungalow with sound bones and a dated kitchen, a Southside brick ranch that needs a roof and HVAC, or a Woodland Heights frame house that has not been touched in decades. For buyers who would rather renovate than compete for move-in-ready homes, a 203(k) rolls the purchase and the repairs into one FHA mortgage.

Genstone Construction carries FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor standing and works with buyers, their agents and their lenders in Richmond to write bids that fit the program, coordinate with the HUD consultant on Standard loans, and complete the work through the draw process the lender administers. Our bids are detailed enough for underwriting and realistic enough to finish within budget.

sections.h2: Standard or Limited for a Richmond house
sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) covers non-structural repairs up to $75,000, which suits many Southside ranches and Northside homes that need a kitchen, a bath, a roof, HVAC, windows or flooring. It does not allow structural work, so a house with sagging joists, a failing foundation wall or a rear addition that needs rebuilding points toward the Standard program.

The Standard 203(k) requires at least $5,000 in eligible repairs and a HUD-approved 203(k) consultant who writes the work write-up and inspects draws. It is the right fit for older Richmond houses where the crawlspace framing, a full rewire through plaster, or chimney and masonry repair are part of the job.

During our review we tell the buyer and agent which program the house likely needs. Choosing Limited on a house that actually needs sill and joist replacement creates trouble mid-project, so that decision should come from someone who has been in the crawlspace, not from the listing photos.

Southside brick ranches are often the cleanest 203(k) candidates. They are single-story, built on crawlspaces with straightforward framing, and their common needs, like roof, HVAC, kitchen, bath and windows, fit within the Limited program.

Northside and Manchester frame houses offer more space and character but bring more risk: knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, termite damage at the sills and porch structure that has rotted. These usually call for the Standard program and a contingency reserve the lender will require.

Fan and Church Hill rowhouses can work, but historic district review adds time for exterior items, and box gutter and masonry repair can be significant. Buyers should plan for that and expect a longer path to closing if exterior changes need a Certificate of Appropriateness. Condition matters too: FHA's minimum property standards mean issues like peeling lead paint, missing handrails or unsafe electrical have to be corrected as part of the loan, and we include them in the bid.

sections.h2: How a Richmond 203(k) bid turns into draws
sections.body:
On a Standard 203(k), the HUD consultant prepares the work write-up, and our bid follows that document line by line so the lender can match them. On a Limited loan, our bid is the primary scope document. Either way, we include specific materials, quantities and labor, not a lump sum, because lenders and appraisers need to understand what the money buys.

After closing, renovation funds sit in an escrow account managed by the lender. Draws are released as work is completed and inspected, through the consultant on Standard loans. That fits Genstone's normal model: no upfront payment from the buyer, draws tied to finished work, and final payment after completion and approval.

Our field manager handles permits with the city's Department of Planning and Development Review, schedules inspections and keeps the buyer and agent informed with photos and milestones. For buyers who cannot move in until the house is livable, that visibility matters as much as the work itself.

faqs.q: Can a Richmond buyer use a Limited 203(k) on a Northside bungalow?
faqs.a: Possibly. If the house needs only non-structural work, like a kitchen, bath, roof, HVAC and flooring, and the total stays within the $75,000 Limited cap, the Limited program can work. If the crawlspace reveals rotted sills or joists that need replacement, that is structural and points to the Standard program. We confirm which applies during our walkthrough before the bid is submitted.

faqs.q: Do you work with the buyer's lender and HUD consultant in Richmond?
faqs.a: Yes. On Standard loans, we coordinate with the consultant so our bid matches the work write-up and the draw schedule follows the consultant's inspections. We send lenders the documentation they ask for, including licenses, insurance and detailed bids, and respond to revisions quickly so the closing date does not slip. Agents get a single contact, the assigned field manager, for scheduling access and answering buyer questions about the scope.

faqs.q: How does historic district review affect a 203(k) in Church Hill?
faqs.a: If the scope includes exterior changes visible from the street, like windows, porches or roofing materials, those need approval from the Commission of Architecture and Historic Review before work begins. That adds time and should be reflected in the loan timeline. Interior work can usually proceed after closing while exterior approval is pending. Repairing original windows rather than replacing them often simplifies the approval and suits the house.

reo-renovation.title: REO and Bank-Owned Renovation in Richmond, VA | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO renovations in Richmond for banks, servicers and GSEs: vacant-house securing, crawlspace mold, freeze damage, code violations and draw documentation.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Richmond
reo-renovation.intro:
Vacant houses in Richmond deteriorate in ways specific to the city's building stock. A rowhouse with a failed box gutter can rot through its cornice in one wet season. A crawlspace with no ventilation and no heat breeds mold on joists within months. Copper plumbing and HVAC equipment draw theft, and older frame houses on Northside and Southside attract code complaints when the yard and porch go unmaintained.

Genstone Construction works with banks, mortgage servicers, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises to bring Richmond REO properties back to marketable condition. We are a preferred contractor for GSEs, and our process emphasizes documentation: photo-backed scopes, line-item estimates, permits and inspection results, and lien waivers from every trade. Genstone Field Services handles securing, preservation and inspections when a property needs attention before renovation starts.

sections.h2: What vacancy does to Richmond houses
sections.body:
The first walkthrough of a Richmond REO usually reveals water. Box gutters and rear roofs on rowhouses leak into ceilings and walls once nobody is there to notice. Crawlspaces in older frame houses stay damp, and without air conditioning running, humidity climbs inside the house, producing mold on drywall, subfloors and framing.

Winter adds its own damage. Richmond does not get deep cold often, but a hard freeze in an unheated house can split pipes in exterior walls and crawlspaces. When water stays on after a split, the result is collapsed ceilings and saturated floors discovered weeks later.

Vacancy also brings theft and vandalism, especially of copper, HVAC condensers and appliances. And older houses with deferred maintenance tend to draw code enforcement attention for overgrown lots, unsecured openings and damaged porches. Each of those conditions changes the scope, so we document them in detail during the initial inspection with photos tied to each line item.

sections.h2: Scoping for disposition, not just repair
sections.body:
Servicers and asset managers need to decide between selling as-is, light repair or full renovation. In Richmond, that decision depends heavily on the neighborhood. A house in the Fan or Church Hill may justify a careful renovation because restored comparables sell well. A Southside ranch might need only safety, systems and cosmetic repairs to sell to an owner-occupant or a rental buyer.

We write REO scopes in tiers where that helps the decision: a baseline safety and code package, a marketable-condition package and, where the comps support it, a fuller renovation. Each tier lists labor, materials and the draw schedule. Dumpster and debris costs, which are significant on houses with years of abandoned contents, are included in the estimate rather than billed later.

Where FHA financing matters to the eventual buyer pool, we flag the conditions that would block an FHA appraisal, like peeling paint on pre-1978 houses, missing handrails or inoperable systems, so the asset manager can decide whether to correct them before listing.

sections.h2: Permits, compliance and documentation for Richmond REO
sections.body:
Institutional clients need a clean paper trail. Every Richmond REO job includes permit applications with the Department of Planning and Development Review for electrical, plumbing, mechanical and structural work, inspection results, and lien waivers from contractors and suppliers. Contractors are licensed through Virginia's Board for Contractors and carry insurance that meets client requirements.

If the city has issued code violations against a property, we address them in the scope and work with the inspector to close them out. Properties in Old and Historic Districts need exterior work reviewed before it starts, which we build into the schedule so the asset does not sit longer than necessary.

Our field manager reports progress with photos and milestone updates through the job. That allows servicers and GSE vendors to verify work and release draws without sending their own inspectors for every milestone, and it gives the listing agent a complete record of repairs to share with buyers.

faqs.q: Do you secure and winterize Richmond REO properties before renovation?
faqs.a: Genstone Field Services handles property preservation, including securing openings, winterization, debris removal and inspections. That keeps a vacant Richmond house from deteriorating further while the asset manager decides on a disposition strategy. When renovation is approved, Genstone Construction takes over with a full scope, and the preservation records become part of the property file. Any freeze or moisture damage found during preservation visits is noted with photos and dates.

faqs.q: Can you clear open code violations on a bank-owned house in Richmond?
faqs.a: Yes. We review any violations issued by the city, include the required corrections in the scope, and coordinate with the inspector to close them once work is complete. Common items on older Richmond houses include damaged porches and steps, unsecured openings, exterior paint and overgrown lots. Clearing violations before listing usually helps marketing and closing, since buyers and their lenders are wary of inheriting open enforcement cases.

faqs.q: How do you document REO work for servicers and GSEs?
faqs.a: Each scope item has before photos, and each completed milestone has after photos and any related inspection results. Permits, lien waivers and contractor credentials are collected and delivered with billing. The format is designed so asset managers and GSE vendors can verify work remotely and release funds without additional site visits. If a client uses its own reporting template or portal, the field manager submits updates in that format instead.
